cue: How do you wish someone a merry Christmas?

es.example: Nos vemos en enero. ¡Feliz Navidad a toda la familia!
es.exampleTranslation: See you in January. Merry Christmas to all the family!

it.example: Ci vediamo a gennaio. Buon Natale a tutta la famiglia!
it.exampleTranslation: See you in January. Merry Christmas to all the family!

bridge.note: The adjective is the whole lesson, and it is not a one-off. Spanish wishes you a HAPPY anything — feliz Navidad, feliz cumpleaños, feliz año — while Italian wishes you a GOOD one: buon Natale, buon compleanno, buon anno. Learn the pair here and it pays out across every greeting in the calendar. The nouns diverge further back than they look: Italian Natale comes from Latin natalis, the adjective meaning 'relating to birth', while Spanish Navidad comes from nativitatem, nativity. Cousins, not the same word — which is why Spanish still has a separate adjective natal for birth, and Italian does not.

interference.es_to_it: 'Felice Natale' is not wrong Italian so much as not the greeting — Italians say buon Natale, and the reflex to reach for felice will mark you out every December. The same swap applies right down the list: buon compleanno, buon anno, buon viaggio, buona fortuna.
interference.it_to_es: Spanish takes feliz, not 'buena Navidad'. Note the noun too: Spanish Navidad is grammatically feminine and often plural in set phrases (felices Navidades), where Italian Natale is masculine singular and stays that way.
